The Seller's Declaration
Introduction
In Quebec, a seller has legal obligations toward the buyer, notably not to hide defects. The seller's declaration is the tool that protects you… provided it's filled out honestly and completely.
This guide explains the legal warranty of quality, the notion of a latent defect, the role of the seller's declaration, and how to reduce your risk of a lawsuit after the sale.
Informational content, not legal advice: validate your situation with your broker and your notary. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

The seller's declaration isn't a formality: it's your shield against lawsuits after the sale. This guide explains the legal warranty, how to fill out the declaration to your advantage, reduce your risk and react if a problem arises.
The through-line: transparency protects the seller as much as the buyer.
The legal warranty of quality
Understanding what the seller commits to by default.
Understanding what the seller commits to by default.

In Quebec, a real estate sale generally comes with a legal warranty of quality: the seller guarantees the property is free of latent defects that would make it unfit for its use or diminish its usefulness so much that the buyer wouldn't have bought it, or not at that price.

A latent defect is a serious defect, not apparent on a normal examination, existing before the sale and unknown to the buyer. If such a defect appears after the sale, the buyer may have recourse against the seller.

By default, a sale comes with a legal warranty of quality: you're answerable for latent defects that made the property unfit for its use. Understanding it means grasping why transparency protects the seller as much as the buyer.
Emilie's tip

Selling “without legal warranty, at the buyer's own risk” exists, but it changes everything for the buyer (and often the price). Never include such a clause without understanding its consequences with your notary.
The seller's declaration
Using this transparency tool to your advantage.
Using this transparency tool to your advantage.

The seller's declaration is a form where you record what you know about the property: past infiltration, repairs, renovations (with or without permits), known problems, presence of vermiculite, a tank, etc. Well filled out, it informs the buyer and strongly reduces the risk of a dispute.
Disclose what you know, honestly and completely.
Conceal nothing: hiding a known problem is the best way to expose yourself to a lawsuit.
When in doubt about a point, better to mention it than ignore it.

The seller's declaration is your transparency tool: you record what you know (repairs, incidents, infiltration, disputes). Well filled out, it strongly reduces your risk of a lawsuit, because the buyer buys with full knowledge.
Emilie's tip
Transparency is your best insurance. An informed buyer who buys with full knowledge has far less recourse than one who discovers a problem you knew about and didn't declare.
Reducing your risk of a lawsuit
Protecting yourself before, during and after the sale.
Protecting yourself before, during and after the sale.
Gather your proof: repair invoices, permits, expert reports.
Encourage the buyer to have an inspection: a defect “apparent” on a normal inspection isn't a latent defect.
Answer questions honestly and make no false statements.
Keep a copy of all the documents and the signed declaration.
A complete file and full transparency are your best bulwarks against a claim after the sale.
Reduce your risk upfront: gather invoices, permits, reports and warranties; declare any known problem; keep proof. A complete file is your best defence if a dispute arises after the sale.
Emilie's tip
Keep all your invoices and reports, even after the sale. If a dispute arises, proving that you repaired properly or disclosed a problem makes all the difference.
What to do if a problem arises
Reacting correctly to a claim.
Reacting correctly to a claim.

If a buyer invokes a latent defect after the sale, they generally must notify you (often in writing) and give you the chance to observe the problem before undertaking any work. Don't react in a panic.
Consult a professional quickly (notary, lawyer) to know your rights.
Don't admit or settle anything hastily without advice.
Rely on your declaration and your proof.

If a buyer invokes a latent defect after the sale, the procedure matters: they generally must notify you quickly and let you observe before doing any work. Don't react alone in a panic — document and consult before committing.
Emilie's tip
Faced with a claim, the worst reaction is to panic and act alone. Quick legal advice keeps you from admitting a liability you may not have.
